person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Mathematical formulae for the measures are presented, as are methods for calculating the measures with lookup tables, computer software specifically developed for SDTapplications, and gen eral purpose computer software (including spreadsheets and statistical analysis software).

span.label: signal detection theory measures of sensitivity and response bias
span.quote: Signal detection theory (SDT) may be applied to any area of psychology in which two different types of stimuli must be discriminated.

span.label: review
span.quote: We begin with a brief overview of SOT, including a description of its performance measures.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Signal detection theory is underused because textbooks describe the theory but omit the computational methods needed to implement it.
span.quote: One possible reason for this apparent underutilization of SOT is that relevant textbooks rarely describe the methods needed to implement the theory.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Moving the criterion shifts hit and false-alarm rates together, so a liberal criterion inflates both; only reducing the overlap of the signal and noise distributions can raise hits while lowering false alarms.
span.quote: The only way to increase the hit rate while reducing the false-alarm rate is to reduce the overlap between the signal and the noise distributions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Ordinary least squares yields biased ROC slope and intercept estimates because it assumes only one variable carries error, while both rate z scores are measured with sampling error.
span.quote: In rating tasks, the empirically determined hit and false-alarm rates both contain sampling error, so OLS provides biased estimates of the slope and intercept.

span.label: Textbooks describe the theory and then decline to give the calculation - the paper quotes one concluding a nine-page treatment with the statement that the measures can be calculated by a procedure it will not discuss. Fewer than half the studies that could use SDT do.
span.term: a theory is under-used because its methods are omitted, not doubted
span.quote: One possible reason for this apparent underutilization of SOT is that relevant textbooks rarely describe the methods needed to implement the theory. A typical example is Goldstein's (1996) popular perception textbook, which concludes a nine-page description of SOT with the statement that measures prescribed by SOT "can be calculated ... by means of a mathematical procedure we will not discuss here

span.label: The two assumptions d-prime rests on cannot be tested in the task where d-prime is most used; rating tasks are required instead.
span.note: what this limits: a d-prime computed from a yes/no task: the paper states the d-prime assumptions cannot actually be tested in yes/no tasks and that rating tasks are required to test them
span.quote: We call these the d' assumptions. The assumptions cannot ac tually be tested in yes/no tasks; rating tasks are required for this purpose.

span.label: One of the two assumptions is singled out as particularly doubtful for some yes/no tasks.
span.note: what this limits: d-prime as a pure sensitivity measure in a yes/no task: the paper states the assumptions may not be tenable and that equality of the signal and noise standard deviations is particularly suspect
span.quote: However, for some yes/no tasks, the d' assumptions may not be tenable; the assumption regarding the equality of the signal and the noise standard deviations is particularly suspect

span.label: The common bias measure carries its own assumption about how responses are generated.
span.note: what this limits: a beta value reported as response bias: its use assumes responses are based on a likelihood ratio
span.quote: Response bias in a yes/no task is often quantified with {3. Use of this measure assumes that responses are based on a likelihood ratio.

span.label: d' (sensitivity index)
span.quote: Subtracting the false-alarm rate Z score from the hit rate Z score yields d' = 1.56 (Equation 1).

span.label: A' (nonparametric sensitivity measure)
span.quote: Application of Equation 3 yields A' = .84.

span.label: beta (likelihood-ratio response bias measure)
span.quote: Response bias in a yes/no task is often quantified with {3. Use of this measure assumes that responses are based on a likelihood ratio.

span.label: regression (ordinary least squares)
span.quote: The procedure begins by using OLS to regress zH on Z F (i.e., predict the hit rate Z scores from the false-alarm rate Z scores).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The correlation between the hit rate and the false-alarm rate z scores is very high (r = .90).

span.label: ROC curve fitting (slope and intercept in z space)
span.term: ROC curve fitting (slope and intercept in z space)
span.quote: ROCFIT estimates that the ROC curve in z space has a slope of 1.28 and an intercept of 1.52.

span.label: The central contribution of signal detection theory to psychology is that it separates response bias from sensitivity, which conventional measures such as hit rate or percent correct confound.
span.quote: The major contribution of SDT to psychology is the separation of response bias and sensi tivity.

span.label: Despite wide acceptance of the theory, fewer than half of the studies to which signal detection theory applies actually use it.
span.quote: Even so, fewer than half ofthe studies to which SOT is applicable actually make use ofthe theory (Stanislaw & Todorov, 1992).

span.label: Fitting ROC data by ordinary least squares gives biased slope and intercept estimates, because in rating tasks both the hit-rate and the false-alarm-rate z scores carry sampling error rather than only one of them.
span.quote: In rating tasks, the empirically determined hit and false-alarm rates both contain sampling error, so OLS provides biased estimates of the slope and intercept.

span.label: In the worked example OLS wrongly implied that the signal and noise distributions had equal standard deviations, whereas the specialised ROC program showed the noise distribution varied far more.
span.quote: Furthermore, OLS gives the misleading impression that the signal and noise distributions have equal standard deviations

span.label: Because the equal-variance assumption was violated in the example data, the d' values obtained from the five different criteria varied widely, so d' should not be used before evidence that its assumptions hold.
span.quote: This violation explains why the d' values in Table 6 each of which results from a different criterion-vary so widely.

span.label: Lookup tables are an inaccurate route to SDT measures because they force hit and false-alarm rates to be rounded, usually to two significant digits, and some published tables contain wrong entries.
span.quote: Tabular methods have relatively poor accuracy. Some tables contain incorrect entries, but even error-free tables can be used only after the hit and false-alarm rates are rounded off (usually to two significant digits).

span.label: criterion
span.quote: The value that defines sufficiently high is called the criterion.

span.label: hits and false alarms
span.quote: On signal trials, yes responses are correct and are termed hits. On noise trials, yes responses are incorrect and are termedfalse alarms.

span.label: signal distribution and noise distribution
span.quote: The distribution of values realized by the decision vari able across signal trials is the signal distribution, whereas the corresponding distribution for noise trials is the noise distribution.

span.label: response bias
span.quote: Clearly, the hit and false-alarm rates reflect two factors: response bias (the general tendency to respond yes or no, as determined by the location of the criterion) and the de gree of overlap between the signal and the noise distribu tions.

span.label: d'
span.quote: One measure that attempts to do this is d', which mea sures the distance between the signal and the noise means in standard deviation units.

span.label: the d' assumptions
span.quote: SDT states that d' is unaffected by response bias (i.e., is a pure measure of sensitivity) if two assumptions are met regarding the decision variable: (1) The signal and noise distributions are both normal, and (2) the signal and noise distributions have the same standard deviation. We call these the d' assumptions.

span.label: c (criterion location measure of response bias)
span.term: c (criterion location measure of response bias)
span.quote: c is defined as the distance between the criterion and the neutral point, where neither response is favored.

span.label: receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve
span.quote: These ratings can be used to determine points on a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which plots the hit rate as a function of the false-alarm rate for all possible values of the criterion.

span.label: Az (ROC area estimated under normality)
span.quote: When this procedure is used, the ROC area is called A z , where the z (which refers to z scores) indicates that the noise and signal dis tributions are assumed to be normal.

span.label: m-alternative forced-choice (mAFC) task
span.quote: Tasks are labeled accord ing to the total number of stimuli presented in each trial; an m-alternative forced-choice (mAFC) task presents one signal and m - 1 noise stimuli.

span.label: loglinear correction for extreme rates
span.quote: A third approach, dubbed loglinear, involves adding 0.5 to both the number of hits and the number offalse alarms and adding 1 to both the number of signal trials and the number of noise trials, before calculating the hit and false alarm rates.

span.label: over 2,000 — citations to Green and Swets (1966) recorded in the Social Sciences Citation Index, used to argue SDT is widely accepted
span.quote: Signal detection theory (SOT) is widely accepted by psychologists; the Social Sciences Citation Index cites over 2,000 references to an influential book by Green and Swets (1966) that describes SOT and its application to psychology.

span.label: .9332 — hit rate in the illustrative Figure 1 example, the proportion of the signal distribution above the criterion
span.quote: The shaded region of the noise distribution constitutes 30.85% of the entire noise distribution, so the false-alarm rate is .3085. By contrast, 93.32% of the signal distribution is shaded, so the hit rate is .9332.

span.label: 50 signal trials and 25 noise trials — size of the hypothetical rating-task data set used for the worked computational example
span.quote: a study in which a subject observes 50 signal trials and 25 noise trials. After each trial, the subject uses a 6-point scale to indicate whether or not a signal was presented.

span.label: d' = 1.56 — sensitivity computed for the second criterion of the worked example (hit rate .92, false-alarm rate .44)
span.quote: Subtracting the false-alarm rate Z score from the hit rate Z score yields d' = 1.56 (Equation 1).

span.label: A' = .84 — nonparametric sensitivity for the same pair of rates in the worked example
span.quote: Application of Equation 3 yields A' = .84.

span.label: slope of 1.28 and an intercept of 1.52 — ROCFIT's fitted z-space ROC parameters for the example rating data, from which Az is computed
span.quote: ROCFIT estimates that the ROC curve in z space has a slope of 1.28 and an intercept of 1.52.

span.label: r = .90 — correlation between hit-rate and false-alarm-rate z scores in the example, shown still to leave the two OLS slopes far apart
span.quote: The correlation between the hit rate and the false-alarm rate z scores is very high (r = .90).
